maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, a measure of federal state medicine would be in the best interests of the Canadian people.
He said:	Mr. Speaker, when I commenced
the practice of medicine some twenty-seven

Federal Stale Medicine
years ago it was in a suburb across the river from Winnipeg. The residents of this suburb were of the labouring class and were not very well off. It may be that a few of them found no difficulty in balancing the family budget, but I fancy the vast majority had to struggle pretty hard with the essential problems of life.
Those were the old typhoid days, this disease commencing about midsummer and running on past midwinter. There was no question about the doctors being occupied, they were kept busy from the onset of these epidemics until the disease petered out, at which time other infections occupied their attention. These epidemics were a severe test of the resources of such districts as that in which I practised. Sickness is always a deplorable matter to be faced by any household; there is always the immediate possibility of the expense of putting a patient in a hospital, there is the cost of medicine and sickroom supplies, the procuring of nursing help and one thing and another. If by any chance the patient happens to be the breadwinner, there is the double disadvantage of having no funds coming in during the time of sickness. On several occasions men have said to me after a sickness lasting from six to twelve weeks that they were not very anxious to get better, they did not see why one would want to get better when so far behind because of his illness and with no possible chance of catching up. In such circumstances when the patient himself is behind financially and is not in a state of health to take up the burdens of life, no medical man can expect him to come forward with medical fees when he is unable to purchase bread, butter and potatoes. In those days it occurred to me frequently-it may be that the wish was father to the thought-that some controlling body, be it the municipality, the city council, the province or anything you like, might very readily establish some system of public health service which would include care of and attendance on those people, thereby securing and guaranteeing an efficient medical service for such cases as those I have mentioned, and at the same time giving the medical man a living wage. At that time I little dreamed that I would ever bring such a matter as this to the attention of this honourable house. But though, as the years went by, there was not the same, shall I say consideration, for the necessity of state medicine, still I have always felt it would be a splendid thing, whether of a provincial or a federal nature, for the people of Canada. So I am happy to-day
to submit this resolution and my argument in connection with it.
In order to pursue the line of my argument, I shall have to follow pretty closely the written text. I trust in so doing I shall not transgress the rules of the house. The resolution standing in my name reads:
That, in the opinion of this house, a measure of federal state medicine would be in the best interests of the Canadian people.
In bringing such a matter to the attention of the house, one must necessarily make certain more or less hypothetical statements, the rationality of which, however, will, I trust *be evident. Thus, the wealth of any country and particularly of this country was originally purchased, not by gold or silver but by the labour of the people. Efficient labour can be the product only of a strong and healthy body. The wealth of Canada must, therefore, depend on the health and strength of her people; that is to say, Canada's health is essentially Canada's wealth. I have travelled far enough afield to have had ample opportunity to realize the deep, inherited love I have for this land of my birth, the land also of my forbears; yet, notwithstanding the vast expanse of her domain, the fertility of her soil, the beauty of her lakes, the grandeur and majesty of her mountains, and the abundance of her natural resources in fish, timber, coal and minerals, I am bound to say that Canada was never a garden of Eden. No honest person who ever came here lived without toil. From the earliest days of Canada's history to the present, men of courage, men of resource, men of faith, men of industry, men strong in body and soul-these and these only have succeeded and have wrested from this great land of possibilities the treasure which has lain in her bosom. No weakling's country this, but a country for strong men and strong women, and if Canada is to make the best of her heritage we must see to it that her people are strong in intellect, strong in purpose, strong in body and limb.
Ill	health and disease are neither necessary nor inevitable. The natural germ cell is not the subject of inherent disease. I emphasize the word "natural", for nature endeavours to give us all an even start. The vital principle of health that has come down to us through the ages is an integral part of the protoplasm of each living cell which, given a fair chance, shall surely prevail. The living cell begets cells of similar order and the inherent properties of the parent cell are transmitted to the offspring. It actually happens that the characteristics of the parent are reproduced in the child. Intelligent parents

Federal State Medicine

beget intelligent children; musical parents beget musical children, and the issue of healthy, sturdy stock in favourable surroundings will come into life blessed with similar strength and stamina. But if an individual be the product of an unhealthy father by an invalid mother, and begotten in an atmosphere of poverty and distress, one can appreciate the unfair start with which such an offspring commences life. From the beginning of history to the comparatively recent past, survival of the fittest was the rule of life. Weakling baibies seldom survived; delicate children often failed to mature, and at best fell far short of the allotted span. As late as the middle of the last century cholera claimed its victims in Canada by the hundred; smallpox wiped out whole communities; diphtheria left homes bereft of children. Each summer dozens of babies perished. Typhoid fever was more fatal in time of war than the attack of the enemy and in cases of severe scarlet fever one could but sit helplessly by and look for a certain and speedy demise. None but the strong, the sturdy, the virile, might, once taken, hope to escape death in those former fierce ravages of disease, and many of the best were carried away.
Now all this has changed. We hear no more of cholera. Smallpox now is but a mild disease, and though still seen, seldom destroys life. The same thing is true of other diseases. By the march and conquest of medical science all these formerly dread forms of disease have been shorn of their terror and tragic import. By isolation, vaccination, immunization, improved technique and methods of diagnosis, by a vastly enhanced knowledge of the cause and nature of disease, and by many wonderful curative discoveries, the human race is now highly protected from the onslaughts of disease, and the weakling, the susceptible and the predisposed find themselves almost as secure as their sturdy and more robust fellows.

public however, rich and poor alike, have been educated to appreciate their value and to demand their application. Unfortunately, to have the advantage of these aids to health is a costly matter which is in no way the fault of the doctor. The result is that the well to do who have ample money are not affected by the cost of medical service, and the cost is of no great importance to them. The poorer classes, those who attend the hospital out-door department and find their way into the open wards, obtain their medical attendance free of charge, and for that reason the cost is of no moment to them. There is a class, a large class which ranges between the well to do and those who cannot possibly pay for the cost of medical care, who prefer to engage their own doctor and to pay their own expenses. So greatly has the cost of this medical attention increased in recent years that it is often extremely difficult to obtain such aid, and not infrequently following a long illness those people are financially crippled, perhaps for life. This class represents a majority of our citizens. They are the people who form the basis of our society; they are our smaller business men, our tradesmen, our clerks, our railway men, our farmers and so on. They are the people who actually carry on the business and
Federal State Medicine

develop the wealth of the country. Surely if the state owes a service to any it cannot afford to neglect them. For these reasons I would have state medicine accessible to all so that this class might benefit from its operation. I have suggested before that the existing forms of the adminstration of state medicine failed to attack the problem from the right angle. The error however is not peculiar to them, it is general. The practice is to call a doctor only when we are sick. Often the doctor is called only when we are very sick and too often when the illness is too far advanced to mend. A system of periodic physical examination would discover early stages of disease which could often be checked and entirely removed, the person being saved from a lengthy and costly illness, and perhaps from death. These examinations would bring to light many mild defects in children such as big tonsils, bad teeth, adenoids, rickets and defective eyesight, the elimination of which would tremendously enhance the health and prospects of the individual. On the other hand the venereal menace could no longer hide behind shame or criminal indifference.	Such assistance
would replace and do away with all existing systems. It should be infinitely more effectual and much less costly, depending more largely on prevention than on cure, and eliminating overlapping. It should aim to direct and control the health of the whole nation; that is, it should be nation wide in its application. To be nation wide it would have to be national. It should be contributory and compulsory, requiring at least once yearly an exact enumeration and record of the people of the country who would be required by law to report for regular periodic examination. This is the first phase of the scheme, the other of course is the actual attendance on sick persons. To defray the cost of administration a regular percentage tax would be collected from the earnings or income of every wage earner, salary earner and person in receipt of income. This would entitle the contributor and his or her dependents to all the benefits of a system which would be uniform for all. The actual medical work could be carried on by the plan now obtaining with the workmen's compensation boards. Or the government could provide a list of medical men and women regularly trained and qualified for the various services. These trained people would act conjointly in the form of a loose clinic. The list should provide a wide range of choice, but any person wishing special service and attention not provided for by the system could obtain the same. Of 
course such service would be at his own expense. The system could be administered by specially set up governmental machinery or by a system of boards resembling the provincial compensation boards. Indeed, the two might be combined.
This, Mr. Speaker, is a rough sketch imperfectly set forth of a scheme for universal national health assurance. Doubtless it is open to grave criticism and it may not appeal to the serious consideration of many hon. members. Certain it is however there is need for improvement in the application of our most excellent science of medicine, and I can think of no better plan.

Mr. Speaker, the mover of this resolution (Mr. Howden) has put before us in a striking way the great importance of national health. Its importance has not been fully appreciated m the past but to-day it is pretty generally recognized that the health of the people is a matter of first consideration, and that disease means national disaster. The education of the people in health matters is steadily advancing, and we ought not to forget what is being done in this direction. I do not suggest that everything is being done that might be done, far from it, but the fact is that persistent work is being carried on in the prevention of sickness. We must not lose sight of all the benefit societies which assist in care of sickness-the benevolent societies, corporations, companies, social workers and various other organizations whch arrange for the medical care of the people, particularly the poorer sections of the community. I am not putting that forward as a broad, comprehensive plan or as being sufficient. There it is, however. It is useful, and so we have it at the present time.
Federal State Medicine

The mover in his resolution suggests that it is in the interests of this country to have federal state medicine. As we know, state medicine has been instituted and has grown in the European countries. Not so very long ago it was instituted in Great Britain-1911, I think it was. But it has not yet reached the American continent to any considerable extent. It has developed in the older countries because, there, there are such large communities among whom poverty is greater than it is in Canada. But it is coming to Canada; I believe the people are beginning to accept the idea that we shall have some plan of state or organized medicine. I do not say, with the mover, that this will include the whole population. I do not think so. But that is merely one phase of the question. There are many proposals with respect to state medicine, including or excluding many varieties that are being put forward. But with respect to the general question, I have sympathy with the idea of medical treatment being provided in some organized way for those who require it. I do not suggest that it come under the Dominion government. I am supporting and I am sympathetic with the idea that there should be a system of medical treatment in this country for those who need it. Whether it shall be provided by the provincial government or by the federal government, or by a combination of the two, is a different matter. At the present time, as we know, hospitals are under the control of the provincial governments. Similarly, nursing and medical qualifications and board of health requirements are all under provincial control. The mover of the resolution has not discussed the question why it should be placed under the federal government. We must have regard-if I may whisper the word-to the British North America Act, which I know is always suggested as the last resource. I do not think it is the last resource. There must be something laid down, recognized and accepted, as to whose responsibility it is. At the present time, I would submit, this matter is largely under the provincial governments.
I he federal government is concerned with certain health measures, but ordinary medical care is at present under the jurisdiction of the provincial governments. There is no doubt about that, and that is a point which would need to be considered.
There is also the question of cost to be considered. Even supposing it were a federal undertaking, what would the cost be? Nothing has been said with respect to this question, although my hon. friend to my right has given some indication of the loss. Whether 
it was the economic loss or the actual cost of medical treatment I am not quite clear.
I may direct the attention of the house to the proceedings, in relation to this question, of two sessions of a special committee-the industrial and international relations committee, I believe-and I would commend a reading of those proceedings of 1928 and 1929, which I have myself very recently gone through. They give some important information. I believe that in many particulars very excellent evidence was given at those two sessions of the special committee. But what I do refer to is the enormous cost, not only the loss through sickness, but the consequent cost which would devolve upon the country were the federal government to undertake such a system. That, of course, is an important question of policy for the government. At the present time the matter is under the jurisdiction of the provincial governments and I do not suggest in any way making any change in that regard. I do think that we can do much in the provision of treatment for those who need it, but that does not necessarily come as a federal measure. The mover has brought the matter forward very well, although I will not say he has done so fully; the question is such a vast one that it would not be possible to present it fully on this occasion. But it is a matter that must be fully understood by the country, and I believe the hon. member would serve his purpose quite well, having brought it to the attention of the house, to withdraw his motion.

If I may be permitted just a few words on this resolution, it certainly comes as a pleasant thing to be able to compliment a fellow doctor on the other side on a non-controversial subject on which we can both agree. The question of state medicine is undoubtedly but one phase of a much larger question, that of social security, which the people to-day are asking from the state. The question of unemployment and unemployable people and the question of state medicine are bound up pretty much into one larger problem, namely, the security which the people are looking for from the government because of the general change that has taken place in industrial conditions in the country.
Probably state medicine comes forward more now because of the fact that the cost of medicine has increased very materially. That cost is in no way due to the medical men; it is rather a reflection of the advance in the sciences. With that -advance the cost

Federal State Medicine
has increased. There can be but one basic reason why we should discuss state medicine, and that would be to carry to the people of the country the full benefit of the advance that has been made in the science of medicine. And that advance is one which undoubtedly is becoming very costly. There has been a very larg increase in the cost of mechanical equipment. The cost of X-ray apparatus, of laboratory supplies, of laboratory applications and of specialty aid in diagnosis, has become so great as to be almost beyond the means of the average individual. Consequently, the principal argument upon which state medicine can be based is that because of the inability of the people to receive the full benefit of these advances we must make some provision to give it to them.
One of the hon. members in this corner of the house made the statement that medicine was made available to the individual to the extent of his purse. To one who has practised medicine as long as I have among the labouring people, those who earn their daily bread, that remark certainly comes as a surprise because up to this time I believe a sincere effort has been made by medical practitioners to extend everything there is in medicine to the masses irrespective of whether or not they can pay for it. It is rather a strange thing that in this country, and in practically all America, we give more time and attention to the care of cattle, wheat, railroads, roads and most everything else than we do to health. The reason for that apparently is that the medical profession has up to this time made its own way and has succeeded very well in giving the attention needed by the individual. The question of the remuneration of the medical practitioner, while it may have a bearing on the matter of giving a proper return to the profession, is not the basis upon which state medicine can be argued. Considering the amount of time spent in acquiring the necessary knowledge, the amount of capital needed to enter practice and the amount of mental and mechanical effort required, the medical profession is to-day the poorest paid profession. It may be interesting to some of the legal profession, who have to listen to medical men once in a while, to know that it costs the city of Toronto just exactly five times as much to look after its legal affairs as it does to run its department of health. Of course, it will have to be left to the people to decide which is the more important.
This resolution opens up a very wide field and it certainly cannot be discussed in full in one day. The matter is being talked of in
medical societies and among medical men all over Canada. There is a very general desire on the part of medical men to extend to the people generally the full benefit of the advances made in medical science and to make available all there is in medical science and in preventive medicine, which latter is by far the more important consideration, but much of this work is becoming so costly as to necessitate a complete revolution in the economics of medicine.
In industrial life to-day there is unknown ownership and distant control which does not furnish that paternal or fraternal care given to workers in the days when employers knew their employees and when they possessed that sense of responsibility which to-day is lacking. There is no doubt but that the people are looking to the state to bring about a proper organization, to evolve some way of regulating and making possible the application in a general way of all the advances of this science. To my mind, the question of cost does not enter into the matter. Once we admit the principle that the benefits of medicine must be extended to all people, whether paupers, rich or between the two, it becomes then simply a matter of transferring the cost from the individual to the state. It does not make a particle of difference what that cost is, it is a matter of distributing the cost and putting it upon those who are well able to stand it, instead of allowing it to rest upon those who cannot.
I believe it to be well worth the time of the house to discuss this matter, and personally I would like to see the question referred to a committee which could make a study of all its phases. Action should not be delayed; we must in the near future be able to extend to the people as a whole the benefits of all the advances which have been made in medicine.

speechtext:
I
listened with a great deal of attention to the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Howden) who moved the resolution. He deserves the gratitude of hon. members on both sides of the house for bringing this very important matter before parliament. Possibly what appealed to me most in his observations was that they were purely of an academic character; he did not advance proposals which might take definite form in the minds of hon. members. We in the medical profession are
intensely interested in problems of public health. Those whose profession oalls them constantly to the bedside of the sick and the suffering realize to the full what ill health means to the great mass of the people.
For the purposes of this resolution I would divide the people into those who are poor, the indigent class; the middle classes, and those who are more well-to-do, the wealthy classes of our citizens. It seems to me that under our present system the poorer class of people receive just as good medical treatment as the wealthier classes. Through our municipal organizations and public health boards, through our provincial organizations and our hospital services, through the free services that medical men give, the poorer class of citizens are receiving treatment to-day probably as cheaply in Canada as in any other country in the world. No sick man or woman in Canada to-day, no matter how poor, need fail to receive the requisite treatment at the hands of the medical fraternity and in our hospitals if they will only apply for the service. I make this statement without fear of contradiction from any part of the house, that fully forty per cent, possibly fifty per cent, of all the medical treatment supplied in hospitals to-day by our medical men is furnished gratis; the medical men ask no remuneration for it, yet in respect to such service they give to mankind the very best of which they are capable.
The class of people who are suffering most under our system of medicine are the so-called .poorer middle class, those who cannot and do not and will not accept free treatment, who do not wish to be classed as charitable and indigent cases, who are endeavouring and will endeavour, in some way or other, to pay their way in the world. They are the people, it seems to me, to whom some measure of state medicine, or assistance a little different from what we have at the present time, should be given under some system such as is now proposed. For my part I should like to see this subject studied very carefully in order that this class of people may secure, at not too great cost to themselves, adequate medical treatment in times of physical suffering and illness and distress. On that account I think that the federal authorities will have to assume some share in the responsibility for dealing with this whole question.
Unfortunately sickness and disease never stop at geographical boundaries, municipal, county, provincial, or even national. They affect our whole people, and if at the present time we have not jurisdiction under the British North America Act to deal with this
Federal State Medicine

question, it seems to me that some way should be found, possibly by an amendment to that act, whereby parliament would be enabled to act. It would seem that in our fight against sickness and disease our attack has been more or less of a desultory character, that the efforts of the provincial and federal authorities have not been as closely coordinated as they should have been.
I would remind the hon. member for Pro-vencher (Mr. Beaubien), who spoke a moment ago, that when on the 17th of March, 1930 I introduced a resolution in this house asking for federal control over the supply and distribution of radium in the treatment of cancer, the federal Minister of Health in the government of that day crawled out from under the resolution by taking a similar attitude and saying that it was a provincial, and not a federal matter. It does seem to me' that some system or method could be worked out whereby these great problems could be met iby the whole Canadian people, and whereby the federal Department of Health would be enabled to cooperate with the provincial health authorities and other organizations in the fight against sickness and disease.
Mr. G. D. STANLEY (East Calgary) As this seems to be a field day for the medical men, Mr. Speaker, I shall offer a few comments on the resolution which has been introduced by the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Howden).
There can be no question that the distribution of the cost of sickness is a big problem, and one which affects a large proportion of the population. In listening to the address of the mover of the resolution, one could not help but feel that the argument he made in support of the view that the whole nation should stand behind what is so important a consideration to our whole popu-Iation should receive the assent of hon. members who in this house represent the people of the country generally.
It is not a question, as I understand it, of objection to the scientific progress which medicine has been making, or to the nature of the treatment being given to those who are ministered to by the medical profession. The big problem behind it all is the cost of sickness and its distribution. When we consider that in this country it is estimated that there are continuously 250,000 people in bed from sickness, and that including that 250,000 there are 400,000 disqualified from attending to their business, we can see that sickness is a big problem, and that its cost is a very serious consideration.

The medical director of the Rosenwald foundation made a thorough investigation of the cost of sickness in the United States. To summarize his report, he estimated that about 25 per cent of the total cost of sickness is accounted for by medical fees, 30 per cent by hospital charges, 25 per cent by drugs, equipment and so forth; and then, coming to the cost of preventive measures used in the United States-and I presume about the same percentage would apply in this country-he estimates the proportion of the cost for preventive measures at one-thirteenth of the total. Taking that figure as correct for Canada, it would mean that the various preventive measures taken by the federal, provincial and municipal governments account for one-thirteenth of the total cost. Then it has also been estimated that at least one-eighth of our population are receiving, without charge, medical attendance at the hands of the medical profession. Financially speaking we have a big problem on our hands when we begin to take medical care or our population over and above the one-thirteenth which is being provided for at the present time by preventive measures.
In considering the practice of medicine generally I think we might divide the subject into two headings: first, preventive and second, curative. Under the heading of preventive medicine we may take all the measures which are undertaken by federal, provincial and municipal authorities. Let us for a few moments consider their development. Going back a few years it will be recalled that there was a time when very few measures were taken by the state in any of its various divisions. These services, however, have been growing from time to time until at present a large list of undertakings is carried on by the municipalities or the provincial or federal governments. When we summarize the quarantine measures, the preventive measures, the clinics, the medical education and the various efforts which have been enumerated by the mover of this resolution, we have the total efforts which are included in this one-thirteenth of the cost. Under the preventive heading we see that the state deals with groups. Under the curative heading exactly the opposite is the case; here the medical practitioner deals with the individual. As I understand it, state medicine can and should be continued and every effort should be made to give all the assistance within the power of the state to measures for the prevention and alleviation of disease.
I am fully convinced that if the state makes the best use of its preventive measures, ex-

Federal State Medicine
tends the services which are being rendered at the present time, continues to develop along the lines upon which it has been developing and takes care of the demands which are increasing from day to day upon provincial, municipal and federal governments, a great service will be rendered to the people. How quickly we shall be able to pass beyond that point, and to the stage where curative measures will be extended to the individual by a physician controlled and directed by the state, is of course another problem altogether. A great service will be rendered if state legislation is passed which in its preventive measures will enlarge and widen the scope of the state, and which will extend to the people those very costly_ services which it is impossible for the individual to purchase for himself or for the individual practitioner to secure. Within the time of hon. members in this house I should think the municipal, provincial and federal governments would find themselves fully occupied in undertaking a great work of that kind. The state can extend its services, as soon as the people will provide by means of taxation the funds necessary for the expensive services required in an extension of state medicine; just so soon may state medicine develop.

Mr. Speaker, the resolution under
consideration reads as follows:	"That, in the
opinion of this house, a measure of federal state medicine would be in the best interests of the Canadian people." I must congratulate the mover of this resolution because it places before the house a question of the utmost importance: the medical care of the health of the Canadian people. May I just state that this resolution, like many others which have been discussed in the house, does not conform with the provisions of the British North America Act. I think that all questions referring to health come under the jurisdiction of the provincial government rather than that of the Dominion government. However, considering the precedents established in this house-and we had evidence of this in the course of the emergency session, in September last, when certain amounts were appropriated not only to assist the provinces but also to carry on road work in order to build a national highway-I think that the mover was quite justified in submitting this question to the house so as to remind hon. members and the country at large that if there be, in Canada, or everywhere else, a service which is deserving of attention, it is that of a medical service as a help toward the conservation of our national health. Notwithstanding
the fact, sir, that this resolution does not conform with our constitution and consequently should not be considered by the Dominion parliament, I am still of the opinion that the government should assist the provinces in establishing-as the Quebec Prime Minister did-health units in order to provide the people of each province with the necessary means to safeguard their health;
I think the Dominion government, in concert with the provincial authorities, should aid in establishing health units throughout every county in Canada.
I entirely agree with the views of the hon members on your right, sir, who stated that the Dominion government should contribute at least one third of the cost in defraying the expenses of these health units.
The tendency shown by all classes of society to claim assistance from the state when it is a question of preserving health, pensioning people who have no need of it-such as judges who receive salaries sufficient to provide for the future-as well as other people belonging to various classes of society who could economize so as not to be obliged to fall back on the state, in order to provide for the needs of their families when they die or become old, is very deplorable.
I make this slight digression in order to remind the members of the house as well as the country at large, that it is time to cease asking for assistance from the state for various purposes which cannot be constitutionally dealt with by the federal government. The Dominion parliament should cease once for all to encroach on the rights of the provinces.
We must first teach the people to live in a healthy state, and should they be without the necessary means to obtain medical care when sickness visits them, it is the duty of the state, but especially of the province, to assist these unfortunate people by giving them the necessary medical care in order that they may later render to society all the services expected from them.

Mr. Speaker, I am in hearty accord with the purpose of the resolution and with the views expressed by the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid). I think a measure of federal state medicine would be of great advantage to Canada. I do not suggest that such a measure should provide for payment of doctors' fees, but certainly unless the rural doctor looked after about a quarter of his patients free of charge, their health would be neglected. This condition of affairs should not be allowed to continue indefinitely. We provide for the education of our children, and the parent who fails to send his children to school renders himself liable to certain penalties. I regret to say that I have seen more children neglected medically than educationally. The hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. McGibbon) has a resolution on the order paper with respect to compulsory health insurance; I think the two resolutions might very well be combined and referred to a special committee for consideration and report.

Mr. Speaker,
coming as I do from a Manitoba constituency,
I,	too, wish to take exception to the remark of the hon. member for North Renfrew (Mr. Cotnam) that in this country no sick person is denied medical attention if he asks for it. In certain portions of my constituency the people are so remotely situated that there is

At the beginning of my campaign I learned that in certain parts of the riding all the children were born without the attention of a doctor or a midwife. I may perhaps be able more clearly to bring home the situation to the house if I refer to an incident which happened up in the Fisher Branch section of my riding. About three years ago a settler was stricken with pneumonia. The lone Red Cross nurse joumed over twenty-five miles to the sick man and transported him to the nearest railway station, where she had him placed on a flat car and brought him to the nearest hospital, about fifty miles away. This was done in a temperature of thirty-five below zero, and the poor man died before he reached the hospital.
Federally assisted medical service is urgently needed in my constituency, and I desire to thank the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Howden) for introducing the resolution. If the federal government could in some way assist any scheme to improve the health of our people, it would be a decided advance socially, and they would earn the gratitude of all those who to-day are unable financially to secure proper medical attention. Possibly if we could not adopt a federal scheme of state medicine we might evolve some way whereby the Red Cross services in the outlying districts might be extended and assisted so that those people in Canada who need medical aid and are without it at the present time might obtain some assistance.

I wonder if the attention of the house and of hon. gentlemen who have spoken in this debate has been directed to the resolution. The resolution reads:
That, in the opinion of this house, a measure of federal state medicine would he in the best interests of the Canadian people.
How many hon. members have considered the implications of that resolution? How many have considered its effect upon the existing provincial organizations, medical and otherwise? How many realize that it means the entire disbandment of the medical associations of the country of private practitioners, and the substitution therefor of the state as employer of all the medical men of Canada? How many have considered that? Yet that is what it means.
I hardly think it worth while referring to a statement made by an hon. member from one of the constituencies of Manitoba as to what I said last year with respect to health units. I have strongly supported assistance being given the provinces in their fight for health, and hon. members will observe in the estimates for this year that there is one grant not * reduced-the grant for the Health department for venereal disease work, which work has been carried on by the federal and provincial authorities. To ask suddenly, after a few minutes debate in the afternoon, to change the whole theory upon which thus far in this country the medical profession has conducted its business is rather a large order. The hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Howden), with moderation, stated his case. No one disputes for a single moment that the nation's health is the nation's wealth. I indicated last- year, as I have always said, that one of the great methods by which we may add to the nation's wealth is to curtail the sickness of its people. There are grave differences of opinion throughout Canada a3 to whether or not the medical service of this country should be nationalized. The hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Gershaw) pointed out that whatever is done in this country must be the result of a gradual understanding by the people of what is involved; and if this motion were to pass in the form in which it now is, it is a direction to the government of Canada to proceed to nationalize the medical services of the country. That is what it means. The hon. gentleman has certainly given no reason to warrant that action being taken. It means that the Dominion of 22110-64
Canada sets itself up as the employer of all the medical men in the country, in -control of all medical services. That is what the resolution means in the terms in which it reads. Are hon. gentlemen prepared to say yea to that? Do any of them desire to say yea?

speechtext:
I say that in no censorious sense because the implications are such that no man, unless he has spent years studying it, can understand what it involves. In England medicine is not nationalized. Some people think it is, but what happens is this. With respect to certain undertakings, certain portions of the population and the state make contributions and the attendance of the panel doctor, is secured. Individuals are entitled to this by reason of the payments made. The medical men retained are paid out of the moneys contributed by employees, employers and the state. Sometimes in Canada, workmen pay one dollar a month, sometimes two dollars, and sometimes fifty cents. Most doctors in Canada have been company doctors and are familiar with what is involved in that work. Have hon. members contemplated what the effect would be of setting up the Dominion as a company and the medical men of the country as company doctors? Have they thought of that? That is what is involved, and I hope the hon. member will realize the advisability at least of not pressing this resolution to a vote. For certainly I do not think that the most ardent believer in state medicine in Canada is ready to vote yea to such a proposal to-day. What will happen and is happening will be a clear and, I trust, proper understanding of the whole situation as a result of the education which is being carried on now by the schools, the universities, and other organizations in various parts of the country which are trying to impress upon men and women the value of preventive medicine.
The most powerful address I have had the pleasure of reading on the subject was made by the late Lord Moulton-I had the pleasure also of discussing it with him-at the university of Leeds; and I heard the late president of the university of Pennsylvania say that it was by all odds the most forceful statement of the case that had appeared in our language. It dealt with preventive medicine and the

Federal State Medicine

effect of education. The theory of medicine has changed in the lifetime of even men of my age. The understanding of the germ theory, the operation and understanding of what is involved in preventive medicine in all its branches, has so changed the outlook of men upon medicine as to make those responsible for government realize their responsibility, first of all, to induce people to think in terms of their own wellbeing, by pointing out to them that disease is the result of a cause, an effect produced by a cause. Medical men, I know, will indicate to this house, as they have so frequently done, that causes are sometimes difficult to ascertain; and to the extent to which causes can be definitely ascertained, the diagnosis of the physician might as well be given antecedently to as after the disease. If it is antecedent, it is preventive, and disease does not occur. Yet, notwithstanding all our scientific knowledge and all the attainments of the years, the fact still remains that we have not been able to discover the germ of the common cold and isolate it and provide a remedy against it. The great Carnegie institute, the Rockefeller foundation, the Rosenwald foundation and others, have spent vast sums of money and paid for years the salaries of the most patient, thoughtful men in laboratories, and have not yet isolated that germ and provided against the recurrence of common colds. We have made a great advance with relation to diphtheria. You will be told today that to have any person die of diphtheria is practically an indictment of the judgment of the person under whose care the patient was. And they will tell you that smallpox, as the hon. member for St. Boniface has said, should be dealt with by vaccination. Yet day after day, in more countries than this, there is being carried on propaganda against vaccination-and very powerful is that propaganda too. Pneumonia has yielded to some extent to the treatment which medical men have discovered in the laboratories, and they have a serum that may bring about very beneficial results. Yet medical men in this house will tell you that it is not always possible to discover the cause of a disease from indications which should be infallible, so that there is uncertainty in diagnosis with the resultant death rates which we have in connection with most diseases. Instead of this great effort, instead' of medical men vying with one another in an ambitious desire to excel-and I apprehend that this would include surgery as well-the suggestion is that we should substitute the state as the em-TMr. Bennett.]
ployer of all. This would be an experiment in socialism which has been carried out in no country in the world but one, and time has not permitted the results in that country being made known to mankind. Can we in this parliament this afternoon declare that Canada is to engage in such an experiment in socialism? I fancy the hon. member for St. Boniface did not intend us to say yea to-day to this resolution. He has very frankly discharged what he conceived to be a public duty; he has made known to this house his own views-that the increased cost of medical attendance and hospital service has made it impossible for the average man to secure the services which he should be able to command. A friend of mine pointed out the other day that his nursing services alone were costing something like $100 a week. The average man cannot pay that much. However, an effort is being made to reduce these charges. One of the greatest hospitals on the American continent has been making an earnest effort to reduce its charges for the very reason mentioned this afternoon by the hon. member for St. Boniface. Other hospitals have followed the practice of charging all that the traffic will bear, of making the rich who are afflicted pay for the services rendered to the poor who are afflicted also. As perhaps this house knows, most of the great hospitals of Great Britain are maintained by voluntary efforts. A constant appeal is being made for the benefactions of those who can afford to give, and the scale upon which these institutions are carried on indicates how thoroughly the problem is appreciated by those who give their money for that purpose.
Without discussing the matter at length; without going into the legal difficulties in connection with the provincial and federal positions and endeavouring to define the relation of one to the other, I would suggest that we do not undertake to make a declaration of such far-reaching consequences without realizing fully what we are doing in the light of all the knowledge that can be secured. Knowledge upon this subject can be obtained, but it involves the studying of experiments and the reading of the histories of those countries that have adopted similar proposals on a small scale in some sections of their communities.
I hope the house will accept the view suggested by the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Gershaw). It must be realized that we have two jurisdictions dealing with the same problem, the health of the people of

Federal State Medicine
the country. The municipality maintains its clinics in the schools for the purpose of ensuring that the teeth and tonsils of the youth of the country are so tested as to prevent the toxic conditions so often produced and having disastrous effects in later life. Then we have the civic hospitals maintained by the taxes paid by the people; we have the provincial boards of health, and the courts have held that the provinces may maintain such boards of health and upon the province alone rests that jurisdiction. We have a federal parliament with power to appropriate to any purpose it may desire the moneys which it collects, and it has given liberal grants in aid of medical education in the large sense of the term, and to assist in the discharge of very onerous responsibilities, to that extent lessening the obligations of the municipalities and provinces.
These matters are not free from legal difficulty. Just a few hours ago the courts in Saskatchewan held that a statute which had been passed in connection with a one hundred per cent pool was ultra vires of the provincial legislature. By passing a statute based on this resolution we would be inviting litigation, because the people are not ready, nor are the medical men themselves ready, to adopt this proposition with all the attendant difficulties which would follow. The hon. member for St. Boniface, a medical man, stated his case with great precision this afternoon, so that we have one medical man who is convinced that the only remedy for the difficulty to which he refers is state medicine, so-called; but that is a far cry from concluding that it is the only remedy to effectuate the end he has in view, the accomplishment of that end by legislation. To pass this resolution this afternoon would be tantamount to saying to the government of the day: You must enact such legislation.
We are not at the present moment prepared to discuss completely the subject matter of the resolution and as the question will become more and more a subject for discussion I trust that every hon. member will in the meantime endeavour to make himself familiar with the points involved in the enactment of any legislation based upon a motion such as that which the hon. member has introduced.

It does not seem

It suggests only that something in the way of state medicine would be desirable, and I submit that there exists in a number of countries a measure of state medicine. It does not mean that we would be sweeping away all the private practitioners, nor does it go so far as to say that we should have a full-fledged state medical scheme; it is a tentative suggestion put forward that something should be started.
The impression has been given that the mover of this resolution (Mr. Howden) is more or less alone among medical men in suggesting what he does in, his resolution. I know in my own city of Winnipeg medical men have been considering the whole field and have come to the conclusion that something of this kind is eminently desirable. It is not my intention to attempt to make a speech on the subject, but I should like to point out that those who have preceded me are in my judgment absolutely correct when they say that under modem conditions the ordinary worker as well as the lower paid salaried man is not in a position to pay the costs involved to-day in hospital treatment or in the obtaining of proper medical services. That is one of the reasons why medical men throughout the country are beginning to feel that something must be done. Superintendents of hospitals are coming to that conclusion and, speaking as one who has been in very close contact with the poorer people, I would say that to-day sickness is becoming more and more dreaded simply because the people cannot afford to look after their loved ones when sickness appears.
I know that many medical men give a great deal of free service, and I think all honour should be given to them in that regard, but there are many people who are not able even to go to the doctor in such a case. You can-

A few days ago there came into my hands through the mail a pamphlet from the Canadian Social Hygiene Council-other members may have received it-containing statements as to the seriousness of the present situation. Mr. CAMERON R. McINTOSH (North Battleford):	I would like to say just a few
words, Mr. Speaker, in regard to the resolution moved by the hon. member for St.

Federal State Medicine
Boniface (Mr. Howden). The resolution reads:
That, in the opinion of this house, a measure of federal state medicine would be in the best interests of the Canadian people.
I would take it from the reading of that resolution that the hon. member for St. Boniface would not want to go the whole way with regard to national control of medicine; that the wise method would be to begin in a small way and develop the measure he urges to national proportions. I think there are just three positions which we can take in a matter of this kind. First, we could take our municipal health units or organizations which are linked up with our provincial health organizations and find out the possibilities of those health organizations, municipally and provincially, and develop them to their full capacity. I do not believe they are being fully developed at the present time. I believe provincially and municipally more health work could be done all over Canada and could thus be very much improved and expanded. As a matter of fact I was wondering, if such work had been done more thoroughly whether the present demand for national action would have become so pronounced.
The second position we could take would be to have the closest cooperation between the municipal health organizations, the health organizations of each province and the federal department of health-an ideal stand to take.
Where we would not leave the question of health entirely to municipal and provincial organizations and where we would not have the closest cooperation between the provincial and federal departments of health, there is only one other position to take and that is full state control in connection with sickness and health. That question came up before the committee on industrial and international relations in 1929 as a complementary question to the subject of insurance against unemployment. The resolution referred to insurance against unemployment, sickness and invalidity. In connection with the question of insurance against sickness, this matter was gone into rather thoroughly and the report of that year dealt with it. Evidence was given before the committee by Mr. A. Grant Fleming, M.D., professor of public health and preventive medicine in McGill University, Montreal and also by J. G. Fitzgerald, professor of hygiene and preventive medicine at the university of Toronto. If I remember correctly, the viewpoint taken by both these eminent medical men was that the federal
Department of Public Health should give leadership of the finest possible type to the provinces in respect to the building up of an adequate preventive health organization extending right across Canada, and that it would be well to have an interprovincial conference called at an early date at which this question of building *up a new organization could be discussed with a view to caring for the health of the nation in a way that perhaps could not otherwise be done.

May I refer hon. members to part of the evidence which was given before the select standing committee on industrial and international relations by Doctor J. G. Fitzgerald, professor of hygiene and preventive medicine at the university of Toronto. Dealing with Canada, he says:
What is the situation in Canada, Mr. Chairman, and members of the committee; what is the volume of sickness and invalidity in this country, either attended or unattended? We have no exact or definite knowledge or information with which to answer this question.
That was the thought I had in mind in suggesting the calling of a conference annually or oftener, in order to secure the fullest possible data with regard to sickness and invalidity in Canada. Doctor Fitzgerald continues :
Federal State Medicine

It is true that certain estimates have been made, based upon the experience in England and Wales, and in the United States, as to the volume of sickness and invalidity, and its cost. But I should like to reiterate that we have no precise and definite information, because no provision is made for the collection of morbidity figures. The volume and kind of sickness occurring in the community at all times in large part goes unreporteS.
Secondly, what provision have we in this country for dealing with sickness and invalidity? it is impossible to completely answer that. Some of our resources are, of course, well known at the present time, but on the side of curative medicine there are between 575 and 600 hospitals, general and special, in Canada, with between 55,000 and 65,000 beds. There are believed to be about 8,000 physicians actively engaged in the general practice of medicine, and there are perhaps one thousand in addition in other fields, such as research, teaching, public health, hospital administration and in charge of the direction of medical or lay organizations.	_
The third question is what is the cost of medical care, including hospitalization, dental treatment, nursing, and so on? Here again we can only resort to speculation, to arrive at any idea at all as to its amount.
Then again, the fourth question; what provision for insurance against sickness and invalidity is now available in Canada on a voluntary basis? It is practically impossible to give any satisfactory answer to that question.
So that my own view, in a word, Mr. Chairman, is that a study of the Canadian situation in respect of the need for sickness and invalidity insurance is highly desirable. In my judgment one aspect of this study could be undertaken perhaps by the Canadian Medical Association, and one of the voluntary health promoting agencies, the Canadian Social Hygiene Council, if such a request came from the Department of Pensions and National Health of this country.
Perhaps from this point on, Mr. Chairman, any service I can render to the committee can best be done by endeavouring to answer any questions the committee may wish to ask.
That was the evidence given by Doctor Fitzgerald just two years ago before the committee on industrial and international relations. Hon. gentlemen will note that one of the points which he emphasized was the lack of information with regard to sickness all over Canada and what we are losing by sickness throughout the country.
Another point which he emphasized was the importance of preventive medicine. An ounce of prevention is worth a pound of cure, and Doctor Fitzgerald made it plain to the committee on that occasion that time after time when an individual knew there was something wrong with him, perhaps something seriously wrong, he did not go to a physician because he had not the money to do so, with the result that eventually his health became undermined, perhaps with fatal results. The nation, in the event of his decease, would lose the economic value of that individual, and

remember that this sort of economic loss is continually taking place all across the Dominion.
In closing I would impress upon the Minister of National Health, upon the Prime Minister, and upon the government, the importance of having the fullest possible investigations made as often as possible into the health of the whole population of Canada in order that we. may keep the health of our people up to normal, and thereby be enabled successfully to compete with the other nations of the world. I take it that the object of the mover of the resolution was that his proposal should be interpreted as expressing the desirability of our ever being on the alert and exercising all possible vigilance with a view to building up throughout Canada a fine type of healthy citizen ready to meet all emergencies so far as health is concerned. If that be our aim I believe the discussion we have had this afternoon from hon. members on both sides of the house will enable us to strengthen our position in any plan of national health betterment, and that the time taken in considering the resolution will by no means have been in vain.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very greatly pleased with the discussion evoked by the resolution before the house. Most hon. members who have spoken to the motion have been in entire agreement. A number of other hon. members have partly agreed, having stated certain reservations. I think the Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. MacLaren) agreed with the spirit of the resolution but saw some obstacles in the way of Canada adopting such a system. During the course of the discussion some points were brought up which I might briefly touch upon.
The hon. member for Battle River (Mr. Spencer) stated that the medical men in this country have a monopoly. I do not believe there is a class of men in this country or in fact in the world, who have been less selfish, who have been more at the disposal of their country, or who have devoted themselves more to the interests and welfare of the people than the men of the medical profession. I am told that Socrates once charged his disciples that whatever they learned of benefit to the human race they should not keep in secret but should spread among their fellows

Federal State Medicine
and give to the world at large. I believe, sir, that that is the spirit which has actuated the endeavour of the medical world since the time of Socrates.
The hon. member for Battle River said also that the care of the health of the average individual was limited to the length of his purse. In some instances unfortunately that is true, but for the most part it is not true It has been my experience that any medical man who learned that his patient, though in need of certain treatment, was financially unable to procure it, usually saw to it that the treatment was given. In many cases the medical men themselves have had to pay for such treatments. The various health boards throughout the country at the present time supply the costly sera, vaccines and other medical aids which have been mentioned in the course of the debate. I think in most parts of Canada a medical man finding a case of diphtheria or any case requiring more or less costly treatment could forthwith obtain assistance from the local board of health. If in the nature of things it is possible, the board of health will collect payment for such treatment, but if not the charge will be made on the municipality, city or province affected.
The resolution I submitted to the. house today was prompted by two main considerations. First, a great deal of the sickness by which the Canadian people are overtaken is preventable by periodic examination. The life insurance companies of this country and throughout the world have adopted a system by which from time to time the assured submit themselves for preventive examinations. If such a scheme pays an insurance company, surely it would pay this Dominion of Canada at large.
The other consideration involved in the resolution is that medical service is sometimes outside the purse of the so-called middle class. As was stated this afternoon, there is no doubt that for those individuals who wish always to pay for their own medical care there is sometimes great hardship. If a system such as I have mooted to-day could be put into force there need be no trouble of that kind. Undoubtedly people sometimes accept a degree of neglect because they feel that they have not the funds to pay for proper attention. In Europe state medicine is national. Germany adopted it in the early part of the century. France adopted it at a later time, and before a person may enter Switzerland he has to pay a poll tax. In that poll tax there is included a premium on the health of the person whereby his health is cared for if he should take ill while in that country. I consider that national health assurance is necessary in order to obtain
uniform periodic examinations and to ensure proper treatment where such is needed.
Reference has been made to the excellent work done by compensation boards. Splendid results have been achieved also in connection with industrial insurance. In nearly all these instances, however, only those who are engaged in the industries concerned are insured, and in regard to compensation boards, only accidents and injuries are covered.
The right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) took exception to the resolution on the score that it would immediately involve Canada in adopting the means of bringing this idea into force. I believe that the resolution does, not necessarily imply any obligation upon the government immediately to adopt such a scheme, but merely suggests to the government that it would be well for it to take the matter into serious consideration

I repeat, serious consideration-with the idea eventually of evolving a scheme which would give the people of this country the medical attention to which they are entitled.
The right hon. the Prime Minister has suggested that such a measure would be detrimental to the interests of the medical men throughout the land. I believe I can say for the majority of our medical men that they would welcome some such scheme as this. Of their own volition they have taken it up in the various provinces and have declared themselves in favour of it. The only doctors that would be opposed to it, and have to some extent actually shown themselves to be, are perhaps the leading men in the profession, the men who do very little and collect big fees. I do not see why the adoption of such a scheme would change the whole system of medicine. Nor do I see why it would necessarily do away with the supervision and control of the provincial boards. There is room for both provincial and federal boards. The provincial boards would still be enabled to exercise supervision provincially, while the federal authority would look after the whole Dominion.
The right hon. Prime Minister made reference to a common cold. This is a very frequent trouble, particularly during the winter season. He has decried the fact that the medical profession has never isolated the germ that produces a cold.

I believe that the federal authorities should supervise the health of the people. It is not a difficult undertaking. When the income tax was put in force the government very readily secured a record of those who came within the provisions of the legislation. the federal authorities in making the scheme operative; in other words, he objected that it was not Dominion-wide. But let us consider, sir, that unless a scheme of health insurance were adopted federally it would be useless. To have health insurance adopted by one province and not by its neighbour would be like having two adjoining fields, one dirty and the other clean. If you have one province in which the health of the people is under proper supervision, and no such supervision obtains in the neighbouring province, the health measures in force in the former will go for nothing.
I do not wish for a moment to suggest that this is a political issue. He said:	Mr. Speaker, I think it will require but very few words to secure the sanction of the house or of any government to this resolution. Another serious abuse has
arisen through the carrying on in certain communities of a price war by the undertakers. In my own town, and in several others, the result is that tenders have been accepted for as low as $40. I ask hon. members how a funeral can be properly conducted at a cost of only $40, when an undertaker is required to furnish:
Casket to be black cloth covered, silk lined, and to have engraved plate and six handles: or casket to be surface oak, to have engraved plate and six handles then to be metallic. (Also crucifix if required.)
Outside case to be furnished.
Body to be embalmed.

No undertaker can conduct a decent funeral for $40 and provide all these items.
The system is very unfair. In one place the price is $100, in another it is $40, in other places it may be $50 or $60, which is most unfair to the relatives of the returned men, who should be all treated alike. Whatever price is awarded to one man's relatives should be awarded to those of another man. I grant that in exceptional cases in the large centres funerals may be more expensive, but outside of one or two of the larger places the price should be practically the same.
These are a few of the abuses which have arisen. All our talk about the glory due to the returned men and the justice we were going to mete out to them is highly inconsistent with the revolting practice of trying to get the lowest price for the decent burial of a returned ex-service man whose death has probably been hastened by his overseas service. I cannot see how this house or any government can but agree and declare that from this day on the revolting practice of asking for tenders for the burial of ex-service men shall be discontinued.

speechtext:
I have listened enough to know exactly what was meant. Do not for a single moment, Mr. Speaker, think I am not entirely wise to these proceedings, and most of the members of the house are in the same position. What I said was that the practice that prevails to-day is a practice that has prevailed for some eight years. The Minister of Pensions and National Health (Mr. MacLaren) will state the facts, indicating what has been done and what is being done. Everything that was in existence when he succeeded to the administration of the department has been continued. But there was not any such thing as tenders in the sense in which that term is used; there never
has been in this country under any government and I do not suppose there ever will be. All that was done was to ask undertakers for their fees for performing a burial service and then to select from those whose names were given the one who would perform the last sad offices for the dead. That is the story. Whether or not that constitutes tenders is for the house to say. In my judgment it does not. I do not think it can be said in any sense to be tenders and I would not have called it such.
The hon. member for Lisgar (Mr. Brown) put a question that has been agitating my mind as I listened here this evening. How are you going to do this? Select one person, and say he is to perform the service and let him fix his own price, or how otherwise is it to be done? This of course is a sort of thing that one desires as much as possible to refrain from discussing; it is not the kind of question that should be discussed in parliament. The administration that has been carried on, is as I have said, continued and what concerns me at the moment is whether or not we can properly describe this practice as calling for tenders. I cannot think that is the proper description. If it is a matter of tenders, it should be discontinued. If, on the other hand, it is merely inviting people to indicate what is to be charged in different communties for the carrying out of the last sad offices for the dead, the situation is entirely different.

maintopic: QUESTIONS PASSED AS ORDERS FOR RETURNS

speechtext:
I regret very much, Mr. Speaker,
that the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett), inadvertently I am sure, injected into this debate a note that was somewhat unfortunate. I think the suggestion that was made by one of the members to my right is the only one which will meet the wishes of the hon. member for Kingston City (Mr. Ross), namely that there should be a uniform amount agreed upon consistent with the decency and dignity of these sad occasions. The amount could be determined by the ministry of pensions, and there should be no question at all of rival prices between rival undertakers. I appreciate to the fullest degree the motives that animated the hon. member for Kingston City in bringing forward this resolution. What he has in mind is that there should be no dickering or bargaining in regard to this last solemn ceremony in which Canada pays her homage to deceased returned men who served her overseas. I am sure the house is unanimous in its wishes in that respect, and I regret the note that has been injected into
Burial of Ex-Service Men

the debate by the Prime Minister. Tender for furnishing funerals of ex-soldiers and sailors for period of one year.
Burial of Ex-Service Men

I objected that this form set up a system of competition, with the result that there were established in various places such low rates that the proper requirements could not possibly be met. And the result, whether hon. members have heard of it or not, is that many complaints have been referred to me to the effect that whereas in one place the relatives of ex-service men were being granted the sum of $40 to assist in paying for the funeral of a deceased, in another place they were receiving $80. That is unfair. I appeal to the wisdom and the judgment of every hon. member in this house: I do not consider that fair treatment. We are setting up competition. The undertaker who received this order submitted a tender of $65. That was not accepted. I know for a fact that the amount accepted by the department was $40, and that was due to what I call local competition.
I do not want to introduce patronage into this question, but I do say that if you elmin-ate tendering and competition you can establish a fair price, and any undertaker who is a friend of the relatives of the deceased should have the privilege of burying that deceased. Under this system I know that that has been objected to in certain places. This, I think, is due to a misinterpretation of the regulations. I believe, however, that in all cases the undertaker who is a friend of the relatives of the deceased should be the person to bury that deceased ex-service man. And that should be the practice, without partisanship and without patronage. There should be a fixed price. Someone has asked, "Why not make the renumeration $100?" I care not what it is, so long as you provide a suitable casket and a proper funeral. But I submit, notwithstanding anything that has been said, that no undertaker can provide a decent funeral for a deceased soldier for forty dollars.

There is a despatch of the Canadian Press, dated October 3, 1930, to the effect that the government has decided to extend until March 31, 1932, transportation at the special rate of $3 a ton in winter and S2.10 in summer time of the coal of Nova Scotia to the markets of Quebec and Ontario.
The matter has been discussed before the Board of Commissioners, who had it under consideration in October. The rates on coal are pretty high. For example, from Sydney, Nova Scotia, to Edmundston, New Brunswick, it is $2.50 per net ton; from Pictou, Nova Scotia, to Edmundston, it is $3.10; from Sydney, Nova Scotia, to Riviere du Loup, Quebec, it is $2.90; from Pictou to Riviere du Loup, $3.60. With respect to the last, under orders in council P.C. 539 and P.C. 2256, the rate will be $3 per ton until April 16, 1931. This appears in a letter I have received from the secretary of the Board of Railway Commissioners, and I understand that the reduction has been extended for some time. Now, the rate for the transportation of coal by water is entirely different. The water haul per ton on coal from Cape Breton and Nova Scotia costs at the present time around 90 cents per ton.
The county council of Temiscouata are in entire accord with the contents of this resolution. Some twenty years ago plans and surveys were made by the Department of Public Works of Canada for the development of the harbour of Riviere du Loup. This city i3 located about 120 miles east of Quebec on the south shore of the St. Lawrence river and would provide an ideal distributing point for coal. At the present time it is a divisional point of the Atlantic and central regions of the Canadian National Railways, as well as the terminus of the railway which runs from Riviere du Loup to Edmundston-and Connor, New Brunswick, on the Maine boundary.
On January 12, 1926, Mr. J. H. Mailloux, alderman of Riviere du Loup, wrote me that the Canadian National Railways had posted
a notice to the effect that the railway was prepared to sell the site of -the branch line from Riviere du Loup station to Riviere du Loup point. He asked me to take this matter up with the railway company in an endeavour to induce them to retain possession of this line. With the permission of the house, I will have this letter put on Hansard. It is as follows:
Mr. J. Frs. Pouliot, M.P.,
Ottawa, Ont.
Dear Mr. Pouliot,-
I have just seen in the post office here a notice posted by the Canadian National Railways, advertising for sale by tender, either by parcel or on bloc, the old Intercolonial branch line right of way which extends to La Pointe de la Riviere-du-Loup. A blue print attached to said notice indicates the route used in the past, with the names of owners whose lands were encroached upon by this branch line. This blue print bears the following description which may help you to locate it. at the Department of Railways and Canals: Wuth Plan 8098 Cor. File 3-2-347.
I believe that it is in the interest of our city and district, in general, that the government should not sell this land for which it will receive very little, because no one except the interested farmers will give it a thought. I therefore contend that the government should keep this land such as it is, the cost of the upkeep should be very little, if anything, and later should our town expand and the port be utilized, we shall need a branch line to carry wood, coal, etc., which will pass through our port. Should the government dispose of this narrow strip of land, everything will have to be done over again later in order to reestablish these means of communication with the wharf.
I therefore trust, Mr. Pouliot, that you will take the necessary steps to insure that this proposed sale will remain in abeyance for the present, and as previously stated, should this light of way be needed later, the cost will be lessened since only the sleepers and rail, so to speak, will have to be laid.
Thanking you in anticipation, I remain, Yours truly,
J. H. Maillaux,
Manager.
St. Lawrence Furniture Co.
I received another letter under the same date from the mayor of Riviere du Loup to the same effect. He enclosed a copy of the notice, and with the permission of the house I will put the letter and the notice on Hansard. They are as follows:
Dear Sir,

Enclosed please find copies of notices posted in public buildings here as well as in the city of Quebec. The government or the railway commission intend to sell the strip of land on the main road leading to the wharf of La Pointe de la R. du L. over which, in the past, ran the branch line of La Pointe.
My attention was called to this matter by a number of citizens. We are of the opinion
Riviere du Loup Harbour

that it would be preferable that this property remained in the hands of the government, first because such sale would bring in very little; then, if later on, one never knows, the question of developing a sea port here came up, the government would be in possession of the necessary land to construct the railway; while, if the land is sold, that might be brought up as an objection and perhaps as a real obstacle in realizing this scheme,
I believe that your views on this question agree with ours, it would therefore be in the interests of the town and county that you take up this matter, and, if possible, with the assistance of the proper authorities, prevent the sale of this land. I think that this letter represents the views of the entire population here, should it be of any help, you may make free use of it to foster the interests of our locality.
Believe me.
Yours truly,
C. M. E. Dube,
Mayor.
