Atlantic Region, C.N.R. Then on January 23,1926, I received a letter from the president of the chamber of commerce of the city of Riviere du Loup. This letter was to the same effect; it asked that I discuss this matter with the Canadian National Railways in an endeavour to induce them to retain possession of that branch line. A resolution was enclosed and with the permission of the house I will put this letter and resolution on Hansard. The letter follows:
Dear Sir,-[DOT]
Please find attached copy of a resolution of the Chamber of Commerce of Riviere-du-Loup opposing the sale of land located at the Pointe and requesting the railway management to retain possession of that property.
The resolution was transmitted to Sir Henry Thornton, and this Chamber in opposing this sale, relies on your support in regard to which 
you must already have received protests from the council.
Yours truly,
The Chairman of the Chamber of Commerce of Riviere-du-Loup,
Horace Cimon.
This is the resolution:
Whereas the sea port of Riviere-du-Loup has never received from the government the development which its importance and economic situation should command;
Whereas this Chamber of Commerce has, on numerous occasions, earnestly requested the government to carry out this development;
Whereas the reports of engineers in the Public Works Department have justified the requests of this chamber;
Whereas to give effect to said reports, plans were prepared to give the port of Riviere-du-Loup the necessary development, and that in 1914 tenders were on the eve of being asked to carry out the proposed development;
Whereas the changed economic conditions brought on by the European war postponed indefinitely the carrying out of said work, but that this chamber intends to renew its requests to have the work executed the moment that conditions warrant its doing so again;
Whereas one of the essential factors of this development was the then existing branch line of the state railways and known as the Pointe branch line;
Whereas the management of the state railways, although having had the rails of said branch line removed a few years ago, nevertheless remained owner of the land of said branch line;
W'hereas the said management now call for tenders for the purchase of said strip of land;
Whereas the sale of said land would hurt the future development of the port of Riviere-du-Loup, and would therefore be detrimental to the interests of the town of Riviere-du-Loup and the economic development of that part of the country;
That this Chamber of Commerce therefore pray the management of the state railways not to offer the land of said branch line of la Pointe for sale by tender but to retain possession of it, and this in the interest not only of the town of Riviere-du-Loup and surrounding districts but also in the interest of Canada as a whole.
I wrote to Right Hon. George P. Graham,
the then Minister of Railways and under date of January 18, 1926, I received the following: Dear Mr. Pouliot:
I have your letter of a few days ago, stating you have been advised by an alderman of Riviere du Loup, that notices have been placed in the post office there, offering for sale, by tender, the land of the branch line of the Canadian National Railways from Riviere du Loup wharf to Riviere du Loup station.
Personally, I am not familiar with this proposition and the only thing I can do is to refer your letter to the president of the board of management, Canadian National Railways, Montreal, who is conversant with the facts, and in a very much better position to deal with same than I. I shall no doubt bear from him before very long.
Yours sincerely,
Geo. P. Graham.

Riviere du Loup Harbour
Under date of March 3, 1926, I received the following from Sir Henry Thornton:
Dear Mr. Pouliot:
With further reference to your letter of January 22nd.
I beg to advise you that the right of way for the branch line to which you have referred will not be sold, but will remain in the hands of the company. I trust this position will meet with your approval.
Yours sincerely,
H. W. Thornton.
Some time afterwards the Quebec & St. Lawrence Navigation Company began to operate a service between Riviere du Loup and northern points, and I think it was in 1927 that I met Sir Henry Thornton and asked him if that branch line was to be rebuilt. I received the following letter in reply under date of April 23, 1927:
Dear Mr. Pouliot,-
After you left my office this morning, the idea occurred to me that it would be preferable that I should have more details as to the traffic which would accrue to Riviere-du-Loup by the inauguration of this new service boat, and more particularly as regards the localities it will call at.
In a general way, I know what it is proposed to do, however I should like detailed information which will give me an idea of the probable traffic.
Is there any one who could furnish me with such information or would you prefer that our agent at Riviere-du-Loup should call on you to obtain it.
Sincerely yours,
H. W. Thornton.
The Quebec & St. Lawrence Navigation Company was carrying more passengers than freight and was operating only a summer service. Due to this fact, and to the fact also that the passengers went to the wharf in motor cars or buses, this matter did not receive the attention of Sir Henry Thornton for some time.
So much is being said about the importance of granting cheap rates for coal shipments that I desire to lay some facts before the house in regard to the convenience of Riviere du Loup as an all-year harbour. The tide is very strong at the point and the ice is carried away by the strong current and does not accumulate at any time to offer an impediment to navigation. The steamship Mahone, which received a subsidy from the Department of Trade and Commerce some years ago, has successfully proved the fact that navigation is possible all the year round at Riviere du Loup. That port is bound to become a very popular winter port because other steamships like the steamship Gaspesia have stopped also at Riviere du Loup during the winter time.
Mr. LaVERGNE:	There are stations at
Riviere du Loup, are there not?

speechtext:
Yes, but the boats do not stop there; I am speaking now of navigation, or to say in French: Je vois que mon ami veut me monter un bateau. My hon. friend is much deeper than is the water at the station, but, as my hon. friend says, we are O.K. I have tried to explain this matter so clearly that I will gain the support of the hon. member for Montmagny (Mr. LaVergne).
The following statement will show the tonnage which could be handled at this port:
50.000	tons Nova Scotia coal for Fraser pulp mill, Edmundston, N.B.
15.000	tons Nova Scotia coal for Fraser paper mill, Madawaska, Me. via Edmundston, N.B.
10.000	tons Nova Scotia coal for Temiscouata Railway Company at Riviere du Loup, Quebec and Edmundston. N.B.
5,000	tons Nova Scotia coal and coke Riviere du Loup. Quebec, domestic use alone.
75.000	to 120,000 tons for Canadian National Railways at Riviere du Loup, Que.
155,000	tons Nova Scotia coal and 5,000 tons Sulphur from Port Sabine, Texas for Edmundston, N.B.
The house would like to know how much it would cost to take the coal from the wharf at Riviere du Loup to the station. It would not be any more than 25 cents a ton, and a reasonable rate for the Temiscouata railway to charge to carry the coal from Riviere du Loup to Edmundston, New Brunswick, or Madawaska, Maine, would be one dollar a ton. This makes a great difference in comparison with the present freight rates, which I gave a moment ago. The house will note also that there are things one cannot understand in these freight rates. For instance, from Sydney to Edmundston the present freight rate is $2.50 a ton, and from Sydney to Riviere du Loup the rate is $2.90, or 40 cents more. From Pictou, which is nearer than Sydney, the rate to Edmundston is $3.10 and to Riviere du Loup, $3.60. It is most extraordinary that it costs more to bring coal from a nearer point than from a further point. But if we take it for granted that it will cost about 90 cents a ton to bring the coal by water from either Sydney or Pictou to Riviere du Loup and 25 cents more to haul it from the wharf to the station at Riviere du Loup, this will mean $1.15 instead of $2.90 to bring it from Sydney, or a saving of $1.75, and $1.15 instead of $3.60 to bring it from Pictou, or a saving of $2.45. Thus to haul the coal by water from Pictou to Riviere du Loup and then by rail from the wharf to the station at Riviere du Loup will cost less than one-third of the present freight rate. If that rate of $1 a ton be accepted by the railway and the Board of Railway Com-
Riviere du Loup Harbour

missioners, there will be a saving of 60 cents from Sydney to Edmundston and of $1.20 from Pictou to Edmundston. That would be a great saving on the price of the coal, because the cost of transportation is included in the price of the material. It would mean a great saving for the companies who distribute the coal, and it would also be an economy for the Canadian National; for the able lawyers of the Canadian National who have appeared before the Board of Railway Commissioners have stated again and again that the Canadian National are losing money all the time in carrying coal. Finally, it would be a great economy for the federal treasury, on account of the fact that if that coal can be hauled at such a rate, the government will have nothing to pay, in virtue of the Maritime Freight Rates Act, to indemnify the company in that respect. Therefore it will be a saving for the people concerned, for the railway, and for the Dominion government, to try out that scheme.
The matter has been discussed several times before the chamber of commerce of Riviere du Loup, and not only is it a matter of importance in connection with the transportation of coal, but I have in my hand a letter from Imperial Oil Limited showing that it is a matter of interest to them also. This letter reads:
March 6, 1931.
Mr. Jean-Franqois Pouliot, C.R., M.P., Riviere-du-Loup, P.Q.
Dear Sir:-
Further re your letter of February 17 in connection with the resolution which you intend submitting to the House of Commons early next session, in reference to the developing of the harbour at Riviere-du-Loup, would say that in the absence of Mr. McKean, we have submitted your request to our general sales department, and are now in receipt of a letter from them, stating that they certainly would be interested in the development of any points by which a freight saving could be made.
It would have to be understood that in order to be of any service to us, it would be necessary for the Canadian National Railways to build and maintain, all year round, a line between their present station and the -wharf.
Trusting that you will be successful in securing the passing of this resolution, and thanking you for calling our attention to same, we are, Yours very truly,
Imperial Oil Limited,
R. G. Plaw, Assistant Manager.
The Fraser Company, Limited, which operates mills in different places in Temiscouata county and also mills at Edumundston, New Brunswick, and Madawaska, Maine, might ship
20,000	to 30,000 tons of paper to Chicago on lake boats at Riviere du Loup via the Temiscouata railway and ex-Madawaska, Maine,

from Edumundston. That paper is at present carried by the Boston, Bangor and Aroostook railway, which, as everyone knows, is a United States railway.
In conclusion, may I stress the fact that something should be done for small centres. I agree with the expenditures that are made in the big cities like Quebec, Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg, and so on, but the small centres should not be forgotten, because, if they are, people will migrate from them to the big cities and the unemployment situation will be worse than ever.
I informed the Minister of Marine (Mr. Duranleau) that I would amend the resolution that is now before the house. In these times of economy it would be pretty hard to ask the government to decide forthwith to construct those harbour facilities at Riviere du Loup for the unloading of coal; but as the plans were made some years ago I would ask the government kindly to see to it that experts are appointed to make a survey of the whole matter and as soon as possible to report accordingly to the government in order that we may know whether the people will receive any advantage from that scheme, whether it will be of benefit to the community, and whether it will mean a saving for the people of Canada without hurting anyone. Therefore I would ask leave to amend the resolution to read as follows:
Whereas the city of Riviere-du-Loup is the most important centre in the eastern part of the province of Quebec;
Whereas the harbour of said city is free from ice in winter, and navigation is possible at all times of the year;
Whereas the said city is a divisional point of the National railways and the terminus of the Temiscouata railway, which links the said city to the province of New Brunswick, and to that part of the National railways known in the past as the Transcontinental;
Whereas the national railways are still in possession of the branch line of Riviere-du-Loup station to the Riviere-du-Loup wharf;
Whereas the transport by water of coal from Nova Scotia to Riviere-du-Loup would be much more economical and would permit of its distribution at a lower cost in eastern Quebec, in the northern part of New Brunswick and the state of Maine;
Therefore be it resolved-that in the opinion of this house, the government should appoint experts to study the matter from every angle and report to the government as soon as possible.
The words that are changed are those last ones:
The government should appoint experts to study the matter from every angle and report to the government as soon as possible.
If the government accept this resolution, may I ask that the experts appointed be men of repute, perfectly independent of the

Riviere du Loup Harbour
Canadian National Railway and of all other organizations, so that the government will be well posted on the matter.

I desire to say only a few words on the proposed resolution of my hon. friend from Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot). First let me say that no government is better disposed than the present one to aid navigation and to facilitate the development of any of our ports. The port of Riviere du Loup, I understand, has had a decent wharf for years, and though the hon. gentleman was a member of this house for a certain number of years he never asked, if I am well informed, for any improvements to that harbour. I do not want to question his sincerity, but it is, to say the least, surprising that nothing was done in that direction when his party was in power, for the hon. member was, and still is, a very influential member of his party. I am sure he sba-es my views on that. It is therefore
surprising that if he asked for something for the harbour at Riviere du Loup when his party was in power, nothing was done, and that to-day, now that we are in power, he is so deeply impressed with the importance of this question. How is it that nothing was done when his party was in power? Surely with his influence and with the help of his friend the premier of Quebec, his great friend, as we know, having a summer residence in the near vicinity, he could have obtained something from his party for the harbour of Riviere du Loup. Surely, Mr. Speaker, if the Liberal governments which have been in power in this country for almost the last ten years have done absolutely nothing at the request of my hon. friend from Temiscouata, it must have been because they thought the time was not opportune or that there was no emergency as to the development sought by my hon. friend.
This government, as I have already said, is willing to encourage the development of any of our ports. We believe that our maritime trade is closely connected with the development and progress of Canada. But the question of developing the port of Riviere-du-Loup is a rather difficult one. The hon. gentleman himself does not seem to be sure as to the advisability of doing certain works in that harbour. First, he proposed in the resolution which is now on the order paper that work should be immediately begun to facilitate the unloading of coal. Later on my hon. friend comes with an amendment asking that a body of experts be appointed to study every angle of that question. So he does not seem to be very sure about the matter himself.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that the question of developing the port of Riviere-du-Loup should be studied, not by a board of experts, but by this government. Surely the former government studied the question, and evidently it came to the conclusion that no improvements should be made to that harbour. But now that the hon. gentleman has brought this question before the house and drawn it to the attention of the government it will be the duty of the government to study the question of developing the harbour of Rivierc-du-Loup. We do not need to appoint a board of experts to study the question. It is our duty to study it. Later on, if we come to the conclusion that the matter is so important that this government is not in a position to solve it, then we will see that a body of experts is appointed. For the time being, I do not see the necessity of such a course, and I hope that my hon. friend, hav-
Riviere du Loup Harbour

ing brought the matter to the attention of the government, will now be satisfied to withdraw his motion.
Mr. JEAN-FRANQOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata): First of all let me give the information asked for by the Minister of Marine (MrDuran-leau). There is a wharf at Riviere-du-Loup, running from east to west, between the mouth of the Riviere-du-Loup and the St. Lawrence river. It is quite a long wharf, extending for half to three quarters of a mile. At the head of the wharf there is a depth of from twelve to fourteen feet of water at low tide. This wharf is quite sufficient for passenger navigation, but the depth of water would be absolutely insufficient for the coal tramp steamers which draw more water.
This matter was studied a long time ago by the Department of Public Works, and I have here large development plans which I shall be glad to show to the minister even before he comes to Riviere-du-Loup, in order to give him some idea of the improvements that are to be carried on there.

It was built a long time ago by Baby Les Quais, before my hon. friend and myself were born. May I tell my hon. friend that when I was elected it was really falling into ruin. I had money spent on it every year in order to put it into good shape, and at one time a contract to repair the wharf was given to a firm of south shore contractors. There was a very dangerous hole in it, and it had to be repaired before the winter season set in. As the contractor was not working I interviewed the then Minister of Public Works and explained to him the whole situation. In turn he notified the contractor to proceed with the work, but his notification was not complied with. I succeeded in having that work done by day labour, and I may say to my hon. friend that it was done very successfully and to the satisfaction of the department. The people who performed the work by day labour did not use the whole amount of the appropriation set aside for the work and they were complimented by the department. That occurred either in 1926 or 1927. Each year quite a substantial item has been voted for the wharf at Riviere du Loup, and the work has been done by day labour to the full satisfaction of the Department of Public Works. The officers of the department were so much satisfied with the work done by the people I had procured that last year when an item of about $22,000 was voted for that wharf it was stipulated that the work was to be done by

day labour by the same men who had given such good service, and not by contract. That is the reason this particular work, involving such a large sum of money, has been done by day labour.
But what happened? As soon as this government took office they chased these men away and replaced them by a foreman who was a thief. I notified the hon. the Minister of Public Works accordingly and he told me to substantiate my charge against the foreman and he would be prosecuted. I congratulated the minister on his readiness to act, but answered him, "I do not want the death of the sinner; I want his conversion." I consider it a matter of responsibility to recommend men who are worthy of recommendation. The point is however that those men were chased away. I said to them,, "You may say you have voted for the Conservative candidate, if you wish, and keep your job; I do not mind." They were too proud to do that however. They preferred to leave their jobs and to be replaced by men who loafed. The whole amount of money was not spent, and I notice there is a revote this year. I have not the complete information, but I know that the foreman has paid-

Surely. I am merely giving some information concerning the work being done at Riviere du Loup. My hon. friend the Minister of Marine wanted to know what the Liberal party had done when it was in power, and I have attempted to tell him what was done then and what is being done now. I believe such information would be a matter of public interest. It is my intention merely to give some information to the house as to what is going on. When there is good work to be undertaken nothing is done, and wrhen something is done it is done wrongly. That is why I take this opportunity of offering some humble suggestions to the government in order that they may improve the situation, if improvement is possible.
As a matter of fact Riviere du Loup is a natural harbour open throughout the year, and coal can be unloaded very cheaply. The use of this harbour means a saving in money to the Canadian National Railways, the big corporations and the Dominion treasury. My hon. friend the Minister of Marine was surprised that I had not made my request when the Liberal party was in power. My answer is a very simple one indeed. Wharves and public buildings had been so widely abandoned during the time the Tories were in power that

Riviere du Loup Harbour
it took me all my time to have them put into decent shape before beginning any new work. Like everyone who is newly elected I wanted first to do some spring cleaning by putting into order everything in my constituency. After that I wanted to try for some new improvements, such as the Riviere du Loup station and a new post office at Trois-Pistoles. Nothing is being done in connection with either of them, however.
I am very proud of my county and my constituency, and I want to replace the building -which has been condemned by the board of health, and have some improvements made. I have given this government every possible chance. I do not wish to have them do this or that in a hurry, but it is well that they should think about these matters. I want to give the Minister of Marine plenty of time to think about it so that he may consult experts. If the whole matter was to be discussed from a constitutional point of view I would accept the decision of the minister, who in connection with matters of that kind is an expert. He is a very distinguished lawyer, and I sincerely hope he will be unanimously elected batonnier of the bar of Quebec. It is well known that the hon. minister is a very able lawyer. In this case, however, the expert must necessarily be a civil engineer, and I ask my hon. friend if he will be kind enough to ask an engineer to make an independent and impartial report about the building of a new wharf, about 1,650 feet from south to north, on the St. Lawrence river, and have some dredging done in order that coal tramp steamers may unload their coal. May I say, Mr. Speaker, that I should be very glad if my hon. friend the minister would accept my suggestion, but unfortunately I cannot accept his-I cannot withdraw the resolution.

He said: We have gone through the order paper so quickly to-day, Mr. Speaker, that I am hardly prepared for this. The purpose of the amendment is stated clearly in the explanatory note, which reads:
The purpose of this amendment is to provide representation for electors resident in the district of Patricia north of the electoral district of Kenora-Rainy River.

For the benefit of the house, I may say that the electors north of Kenora located in this district were denied the vote in 1925 and again in 1926, and the bill introduced at the last regular session of 1930, just prior to the federal election, was for the purpose of giving votes to the miners, labourers and others residing north of Kenora. At the last federal redistribution the territory was cut off on the south bank of the English river, but since that time mining developments have opened up in the Red Lake district, the Woman River district and at Pine Falls. With these mines and with the development of waterpower some 500 to 600 electors were disfranchised during the last federal elections I am sure when the Prime Minister opposed this measure when it was last before the house he was not fully aware of the fact that there would be between 500 and 600 people disfranchised in this country. Unfortunately I had to be absent from the house when the bill was up for its second reading and I was not in position to give the required information.
I believe the Prime Minister was misinformed in the position he took when the matter was last before the house. These people were not permitted to vote during the last campaign because of a ruling given by the chief electoral officer. It is unfair and unjust to deprive citizens of this part of the country especially-if I am permitted to specialize-those hard-working pioneers who are creating new wealth in northern Ontario or in other parts of the country of the privilege of casting their ballots, and I ask that this bill be given its second reading.

maintopic: ARMISTICE DAY ACT
ARMISTICE DAY ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CELEBRATION OF ARMISTICE DAY ON NOVEMBER 11

speechtext:
Mr. A. W. NEILL (Comox-Alberni) moved the second reading of Bill No. 8, to amend the Armistice Day Act.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this is a very short and simple bill. It provides that two sections of the Armistice Day Act, passed in 1921, shall be repealed and the bill of which I am now moving the second reading substituted therefor.
This bill provides that the celebration of Armistice Day shall be held on November
11 of each year and on no other day, whereas the previous act provided that it should be held on the Monday of the week in which November 11 fell. The bill says nothing about Thanksgiving day, so the procedure in that regard will revert to what it was prior to 1921. It will be at the option of the government to proclaim when Thanksgiving day shall be celebrated, not necessarily in November but perhaps in October.
The old act has been the law for ten years, and one would have supposed that what opposition there might have been to it originally would have died out, but on the contrary it has been increasing year after year. The reason why this opposition did not come to a 'head sooner is, I believe, that a great many soldiers did not know that that was the law. Many of them simply went ahead and celebrated Armistice day on November 11 regardless of what day was fixed by law. They are beginning to find out what is the law and there is a general feeling throughout the country that Armistice day should be celebrated on November 11 and on no other day. The only people wiho object to this proposal are commercial travellers who desire to be able to come home on a Friday or Saturday night and have a holiday on Monday. Perhaps there are a few others who would like to go to their homes and have a holiday on Monday, but I would point out that this day was never intended to be a public holiday in the sense of bank holidays and so on; it was intended as a remembrance day for the soldiers, and they are entitled to have it on that day. We never hear of any proposals to have Christmas day, New Year's day or the 1st of July held on the Monday of the week in which tihose particular days fall.
This matter is solely and entirely the concern of the returned men and we as a governing body ought to respect their wishes. It has nothing to do with what other people want, and the soldiers should surely have the right to decide.
I have no desire to take up the time of the house, but I have stacks of supporting resolutions and letters from every part of the country. I have a communication from the Dominion executive council of the Canadian Legion, and they refer also to a resolution passed at the Dominion convention held last November. I have received resolutions adopted by a large number of bodies, one from Mrs. Barnard who represents one thousand women of the British Columbia Women's provincial command. There are others from various bodies in the west and elsewhere, some representing five hundred and more
Armistice Day Act

returned men. In no single instance have I received objection from any soldier, let alone any representative body of soldiers.
I would repeat that this has nothing at all to do with and will not interfere with Thanksgiving day. Thanksgiving day can be celebrated on any day which the government sees fit to name, but the soldiers are asking that Armistice day be celebrated only on November 11. When it is observed on some other day they find difficulty in getting away from their occupation or business to carry on their own celebration on November 11. They regard this day not as a holiday but as a day of sacred remembrance.
I do not believe there will be any objection to this bill from any section of the country, and I trust it will receive the support of the house.

maintopic: ARMISTICE DAY ACT
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CELEBRATION OF ARMISTICE DAY ON NOVEMBER 11
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am thoroughly in accord with the remarks of the introducer of this bill, with one slight exception to which I will refer a little later. I find that it is almost the unanimous wish of the returned men and their families in British Columbia, and I presume it is the same throughout the rest of Canada, that this change be made. Thanksgiving day has always been associated in our minds with the harvest festival, which originated when the pilgrim fathers garnered their first crop in 1641. The soldiers are perfectly right in asking for this change, and I agree with the hon. member for Comox-Albemi (Mr. Neill) that their wishes should be respected.
I received a communication from the Dominion headquarters Of the Canadian Legion, one clause of which reads as follows:
Be it therefore resolved-that we request that the parliament of Canada be requested and do hereby respectfully request it to enact legislation whereby in place of the present Thanksgiving day, November 11 in every year shall be set aside as a national holiday to be known as Remembrance day.
Those of us who gather each year before the cenotaphs throughout the country know that the thoughts associated with Thanksgiving day are forgotten. The sad memories usually connected with Armistice day take away from the joyousness which should prevail on Thanksgiving day. It is the wish of the soldier bodies that this day be known as Remembrance day, and I think we should acquiesce in their wishes.
I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Barber):
That the word ''Armistice" in the last line be struck out and the word "Remembrance" substituted therefor.
